title: Supply Chain & Raw Materials Sourcing
subtitle: Find, compare, check and plan your materials so production never stops for want of supply.
description: A practical, numbers-based course for producers whose business now depends on steady materials. You map your supply chain, rank materials by value and risk, calculate reorder points from real lead times, check and score suppliers, compare total cost, and build a written plan to reduce your biggest sourcing risk.
outcomes: Build a bill of materials and a supply map that shows every critical material and single point of failure
Rank materials with ABC analysis and the Kraljic matrix and choose a sourcing approach for each
Calculate safety stock and reorder points from your own lead-time records
Run receiving checks, keep batch traceability and score suppliers with OTIF and weighted scorecards
Compare suppliers on total cost per usable unit and negotiate using a tested backup
Delegate purchasing with clear controls and lead a 90-day plan to reduce supply risk
audience: Women who already produce goods such as food, drinks, cosmetics, garments or crafts and want reliable, well-priced materials as they scale up.
tools: Smartphone with WhatsApp and a spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets
A reliable weighing scale and a measuring tape
Your recent purchase receipts and production records
Masking tape and a marker for shelf labels

modules.title: Seeing Your Supply Chain Clearly
modules.overview: Before you can protect your supply, you must see it. In this module you list every material in your product, trace where each one really comes from, rank materials by value and risk, and write the specifications and buying rules that every supplier and helper must follow.

lessons.title: Mapping your supply chain from source to workshop
objectives: Build a bill of materials that shows the cost of each input per unit
Trace each key material back through its supplier tiers
Identify which materials are critical to production
Spot single points of failure on your own supply map

blocks.text: A **supply chain** is every step a material passes through before it becomes part of your product: the farm or factory that makes it, the wholesaler or importer who moves it in bulk, the market trader who sells it to you, the transport that brings it to your door, and your own store. When you buy from whoever has stock that day, you only see the last step. Supply chain management starts when you deliberately look at all of them.

At small scale, a missing material is an inconvenience. Once customers, shops or institutions depend on your output, a missing material becomes a broken promise. A supermarket that receives no delivery for two weeks may give your shelf space to someone else. This course is about making that kind of failure rare, planned for and quickly fixed.

blocks.name: logistics
blocks.alt: Boxes being moved through a delivery network
blocks.caption: Every material you use travels through several hands before it reaches your workshop.

blocks.text: Step one: the bill of materials

A **bill of materials** (often shortened to BOM) is a list of every input needed to make one unit or one batch of your product, with the quantity and cost of each. Manufacturers everywhere use it. It answers two questions at once: what exactly do I need to buy, and which materials take the biggest share of my cost?

blocks.title: Worked example: a bill of materials for zobo drinks
blocks.context: Amaka, for example, makes bottled zobo in Enugu and sells about 600 bottles of 50cl a week to offices and small shops. She works in batches of 100 bottles. Prices below are illustrative and approximate; use your own current market prices.
steps: Dried hibiscus (zobo leaves): 1.5 kg at about ₦3,000 per kg = ₦4,500
Sugar: 4 kg at about ₦1,800 per kg = ₦7,200
Fresh ginger: 0.5 kg at about ₦2,000 per kg = ₦1,000
50cl PET bottles with caps: 100 at about ₦60 each = ₦6,000
Printed labels: 100 at about ₦25 each = ₦2,500
Total materials per batch = ₦21,200, so materials cost ₦212 per bottle
Share of cost: sugar 34%, bottles 28%, hibiscus 21%, labels 12%, ginger 5%
blocks.result: Amaka now sees that sugar and bottles together are about 62% of her material cost. A price rise or shortage in either one hits her harder than a problem with ginger.

blocks.text: Notice what the BOM leaves out on purpose: gas, water, labour and transport. Those are real costs, and you will add transport into the true cost of materials in Module 2. For mapping, keep the BOM to physical inputs that go into or onto the product.
Step two: trace each material through its tiers

Supply chain people talk about **tiers**. Your **tier 1** supplier is the person you pay directly, for example a trader at the main market. **Tier 2** is who supplies that trader, for example a wholesaler or a factory distributor. **Tier 3** may be the farm, the processor or the foreign manufacturer. You rarely control tiers 2 and 3, but you must know they exist, because a problem there reaches you a few days or weeks later.

blocks.title: How a material reaches you
items: Farm, factory or importer
Wholesaler or distributor
Market trader (tier 1)
Transport to you
Your store
Production
blocks.caption: A delay or price change at any step travels down the chain until it reaches your production table.

blocks.text: Ask your tier 1 supplier simple, respectful questions: Where does this come from? Who do you buy it from? Is it the same source every time? How long does it take you to restock when you run out? Many traders will answer if you are a regular customer. Write the answers down. For Amaka, the hibiscus comes from traders who buy from growers in the northern states, while her bottles come from one distributor of a single bottle factory. That second fact matters a lot.
Step three: mark your critical materials
A material is **critical** if you cannot produce without it and cannot quickly swap it for something else. Test each material with three questions:

items: **Can I make the product without it?** If no, it is essential.
**Can I switch to another source within one week without changing the product?** If no, it is hard to replace.
**Would customers notice a change?** If yes, a substitute carries quality or brand risk.

head: Material
Essential?
Easy to replace within a week?
Critical?
rows: Yes, many traders sell it, but quality varies
No, her labels and caps fit only this bottle
Partly, another printer needs the design file

blocks.text: A **single point of failure** is one supplier, one route or one person whose absence would stop production. Amaka's bottle distributor is one. So is the label printer if only he holds her design file. The fix for the printer is free: keep your own copy of the print-ready file and share it with a second printer. The fix for the bottles takes more work, and you will plan it in the capstone.

blocks.title: Draw it, do not just think it
blocks.text: Draw your map on one page: your product in the middle, each material as a branch, and each supplier you know along the branch. Circle any branch with only one name on it. Those circles are your first sourcing risks.

Keep your map in a notebook or a Google Sheet with one row per material and columns for the supplier name, phone number, location, price, how often you buy, and the tier 2 source if you know it. Update it every time something changes. This one page is the foundation for every lesson that follows.

takeaways: A bill of materials shows what you buy and which inputs take the biggest share of cost
Tier 1 is who you pay; tiers 2 and 3 are where many shortages actually start
A critical material is essential and hard to replace quickly
Any branch of your map with only one supplier is a single point of failure

activity.title: Map one product's supply chain
steps: Choose your best-selling product and write its bill of materials for one batch, with quantities and current prices
Calculate the material cost per unit and the percentage share of each material
For each material, write your tier 1 supplier and ask them where they get it (tier 2)
Mark each material as critical, medium or low using the three questions
Circle every material that has only one supplier
activity.evidence: A photo of your one-page supply map and your BOM table with percentages

lessons.title: Ranking materials by value and risk: ABC analysis and the Kraljic matrix
objectives: Sort materials into A, B and C classes by annual spend
Place each material in one of the four Kraljic quadrants
Choose a sourcing approach that fits each quadrant
Decide where to spend your limited time on suppliers

blocks.text: You cannot give every material the same attention. A busy owner has limited hours, limited cash and limited patience for market trips. Two simple tools, used by purchasing professionals worldwide, tell you where your attention pays off: **ABC analysis**, which ranks materials by how much money you spend on them, and the **Kraljic matrix**, which adds a second question: how risky is the supply?
ABC analysis: follow the money

List every material with its total spend over a year (or estimate: monthly spend multiplied by 12). Sort from highest to lowest and calculate each one's share of the total. A common rule of thumb is that a few items make up most of the spend. Class **A** items are the top ones that together make up roughly 70 to 80% of spend. Class **B** items make up the next 15 to 25%. Class **C** items are the many small items that make up the last few percent. The exact cut-offs are a guide, not a law.

blocks.title: Worked example: ABC analysis for a uniform workshop
blocks.context: Bisi, for example, runs a tailoring workshop in Ibadan that sews uniforms for three private schools. Her estimated yearly material spend is ₦3,200,000 (figures illustrative).
steps: School-colour check fabric: ₦1,500,000, which is 46.9% of spend
White shirting fabric: ₦900,000, which is 28.1%. Running total: 75.0%
Interlining: ₦210,000 (6.6%), buttons: ₦180,000 (5.6%), thread: ₦150,000 (4.7%). Running total: about 91.9%
Zips: ₦120,000 (3.8%), poly bags for packing: ₦90,000 (2.8%), elastic: ₦50,000 (1.6%). Running total: 100%
Class A: the two fabrics. Class B: interlining, buttons, thread. Class C: zips, bags, elastic
blocks.result: Two materials out of eight carry 75% of Bisi's spend. A 5% better price on fabric saves about ₦120,000 a year, while a 5% better price on elastic saves only ₦2,500.

blocks.text: ABC alone can mislead you. Bisi's zips are a C item by spend, but if the school insists on one zip colour that only one importer stocks, running out of zips stops delivery just as surely as running out of fabric. That is why you add the second question.
The Kraljic matrix: value and risk together

In 1983 Peter Kraljic published an article in the Harvard Business Review arguing that purchasing should become supply management. His matrix places each material on two scales. **Profit impact**: how much it affects your cost and product quality (your ABC class is a good starting point). **Supply risk**: how hard it is to get, judged by the number of suppliers, how easy it is to substitute, transport problems, imports and price swings.

blocks.title: Kraljic matrix
items: Leverage items
Strategic items
Non-critical items
Bottleneck items
blocks.caption: Top row has high profit impact, right column has high supply risk; each quadrant needs a different buying approach.

head: Quadrant
What it means
Bisi's example
Sourcing approach
rows: Big spend and few good sources
School-colour check fabric, matched to the school's sample
Build a close relationship, share forecasts, agree quality in writing, qualify a backup and hold safety stock
Compare quotes, buy in volume, negotiate price and terms
Small spend but hard to get
Zips in the one colour the school demands
Hold extra stock, find any second source, or ask the client to approve an alternative
Keep it simple: buy in convenient lots, reduce time spent

blocks.name: scales
blocks.caption: The matrix weighs two things at once: what a material is worth to you and how risky its supply is.

blocks.text: Single sourcing or dual sourcing?

**Single sourcing** means buying a material from one supplier. It can earn you better attention and price, but it leaves you exposed. **Dual sourcing** means keeping two active suppliers, perhaps buying most from one and a smaller share from the other so the second relationship stays alive. For leverage items, dual sourcing is easy and keeps prices honest. For strategic items, you often have to choose a main partner and invest in the relationship, yet you should still test and approve a backup before a crisis, not during one.

blocks.title: Your scores are judgements
blocks.text: There is no official score for supply risk. Use what you know: how many sellers you have found, whether it is imported, whether it is seasonal, and how often it has been out of stock. Review the matrix every six months, because a material can move. A new local factory can turn a bottleneck into a non-critical item.

items: List all materials with annual spend and calculate percentage shares
Mark A, B and C classes
Score each material's supply risk as low or high, with a one-line reason
Place each material in a quadrant
Write one sourcing action for each strategic and bottleneck item

blocks.text: Most small producers find two or three strategic items, one or two bottlenecks and a long list of non-critical items. Your time with suppliers should go mainly to the strategic and bottleneck boxes. For the non-critical box, the goal is the opposite: spend as little thinking time as possible, for example by buying a month of thread at once.

takeaways: ABC analysis ranks materials by spend so you see where price savings matter
The Kraljic matrix adds supply risk to spend, giving four quadrants
Strategic items need partnership plus a tested backup; leverage items need competition
Cheap bottleneck items can stop production and deserve extra stock or a second source

activity.title: Rank your materials
steps: Estimate the yearly spend on each material from your BOM and sales volume
Sort the list, calculate percentage shares and mark A, B and C
Draw the four-box matrix on paper and write each material in its box with a reason
Choose one sourcing action for every item in the strategic and bottleneck boxes
activity.evidence: Your ABC table and a photo of your completed matrix

lessons.title: Writing material specifications and your sourcing rules
objectives: Write a material specification that a new supplier can follow
Design a small trial to approve a new supplier's material
Set your own non-negotiable sourcing rules
Behave as a buyer that suppliers want to serve first

blocks.text: Many quality problems start with a vague order. 'Bring me good shea butter' means something different to every trader. A **material specification** (spec) is a short written description of exactly what you accept. It protects you when you change suppliers, when a helper buys on your behalf, and when you need to reject a bad delivery without an argument.
What goes into a specification

items: **Name and type**: the exact material, grade or variety, and any brand you require
**Appearance, smell and feel**: what a good sample looks like, and what is unacceptable
**Measurable limits**: size, weight, width, thickness or other numbers you can check with simple tools
**Packaging**: container type, size, sealing and labelling, including supplier batch or lot number where one exists
**Documents**: invoice or receipt, and for regulated materials any certificate the product requires
**Delivery**: where, when, and how much notice you need
**Reference sample**: a retained sample you both agree represents the standard

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.alt: A clipboard with a written list
blocks.caption: A one-page spec turns 'good quality' into something anyone can check.

blocks.title: Worked example: a spec for shea butter
blocks.context: Funke, for example, makes whipped body butter in Lagos and uses about 20 kg of shea butter a month. Twice she received butter with grit and a sour smell. She writes this spec and sends it on WhatsApp to every supplier before ordering.
steps: Material: unrefined shea butter, for cosmetic use
Appearance: ivory to pale yellow, smooth, no visible dirt, sand, fibres or water drops
Smell: mild and nutty. Reject if sour, rancid or smoky
Packaging: clean, sealed, food-grade plastic buckets of 5 kg or 25 kg, with the packing date written on the lid
Reference: one 250 g jar from an approved delivery kept in her store as the standard
Trial for a new supplier: buy 5 kg, melt and strain 1 kg, weigh what is left in the strainer, and make one small batch of product before approving
Result of a trial: 1,000 g melted, 100 g of grit and residue in the strainer, so 10% waste. Her approved supplier's residue was about 10 g, or 1%
blocks.result: Funke can now compare suppliers on facts. The new supplier's butter wastes ten times as much, which she will price into her comparison in Module 2.

blocks.text: Notice that Funke did not invent laboratory numbers she cannot test. A small producer's spec should use checks she can actually do: look, smell, weigh, measure with a tape, count, or run a small test batch. If your product is regulated, NAFDAC or SON requirements for the finished product come first, and your spec must make sure every input lets you meet them. For example, a cosmetic or food producer should only use materials meant for that use, not industrial grades.

blocks.title: Chemical materials need extra rules
blocks.text: If you buy chemicals such as caustic soda, acids, solvents or fragrance oils, add to your spec: original sealed container, clear product name and hazard label, and a safety data sheet (SDS) where the supplier can provide one. Never accept a chemical repacked into an unlabelled water bottle or food container. Store chemicals away from food materials and out of reach of children.
Your sourcing rules

Specs describe materials. **Sourcing rules** describe how you buy. Decide them calmly now, because under pressure people take shortcuts. Good rules are short and written. Here are examples you can adapt:

blocks.title: Example sourcing rules
items: Never below the agreed spec
No new supplier without trial
Backup for every strategic item
Pay on agreed dates
Keep all receipts and records
blocks.caption: Five written rules stop rushed decisions from damaging quality or cash.

blocks.text: Some owners also set a **concentration limit**, for example 'no single supplier provides more than 80% of a strategic material once a backup is approved'. Pick a figure that fits your situation; the point is to keep the backup relationship real by giving it regular small orders.
Be a buyer suppliers want to serve

During a shortage, suppliers decide who gets the limited stock. They usually favour customers who order regularly, pay as agreed, give notice of big orders and treat their staff with respect. You build that reputation in calm times. Practical habits:

items: Share a rough forecast: 'From October I expect to need about 30 kg a month'
Pay on the date you promised, and say early if you cannot
Visit your strategic suppliers at least once, and see where and how the material is stored
Give clear feedback, both complaints and thanks, with photos and dates
Keep personal favours and gifts out of buying decisions

blocks.title: Paying a new supplier
blocks.text: Scammers pose as suppliers on WhatsApp, Facebook and online marketplaces. For a first order, prefer to see the goods, start with a small trial, pay into an account whose name matches the business, and keep the transfer receipt. Be wary of a price far below the market or pressure to pay in full today.

takeaways: A written spec turns 'good quality' into checks anyone can perform
Use tests you can really do: look, smell, weigh, measure, trial batch
Approve new suppliers with a small trial and a retained reference sample
Written sourcing rules protect quality and cash when you are under pressure
Reliable payment and clear forecasts earn priority during shortages

activity.title: Write one spec and your rules
steps: Choose your most important strategic material and write a one-page spec using the seven headings
Keep a reference sample of an approved delivery and label it with the date and supplier
Design a trial for a new supplier with a measurable result, such as waste percentage
Write your five sourcing rules and stick them where you or your buyer will see them
Send the spec to your current supplier and ask them to confirm they can meet it
activity.evidence: Your written spec, a photo of the labelled reference sample, and your list of sourcing rules

quiz.q: Amaka's bill of materials shows sugar at 34% and ginger at 5% of material cost. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A 10% rise in sugar price affects her cost far more than a 10% rise in ginger price
Ginger is more critical because it is cheaper
Both materials affect her cost equally
She should stop tracking ginger altogether
quiz.explain: The larger a material's share of cost, the more a price change moves the total. A 10% rise on sugar adds about 3.4% to material cost; on ginger, about 0.5%.

quiz.q: Bisi's trader buys fabric from a Lagos distributor, who imports it from a factory abroad. In supply chain terms, the distributor is Bisi's:
quiz.explain: Tier 1 is the trader she pays directly. The trader's own supplier, the distributor, is tier 2.

quiz.q: Zips are only 3.8% of Bisi's spend, but the school requires one colour that only one importer stocks. Where do zips belong on the Kraljic matrix?
quiz.explain: Low profit impact but high supply risk is the bottleneck quadrant. The right response is extra stock, a second source or client approval of an alternative.

quiz.q: A new shea butter supplier offers a lower price. What should Funke do before approving them?
options: Order 100 kg to get the best discount
Buy a small trial, compare it with her reference sample and measure the waste
Ask friends on WhatsApp if the price is good
Switch completely if the colour looks right
quiz.explain: A small trial with a measurable check, compared with an agreed reference sample, shows real quality before she risks a full order.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in a small producer's material specification?
options: A laboratory value she has no way to test
Packaging type and size, with the packing date written on the container
quiz.explain: A useful spec contains checks she can actually verify on delivery, such as packaging, appearance, smell and simple measurements.

quiz.q: White shirting fabric is a high spend item with many suppliers. What is the best sourcing approach?
options: Compare quotes from several suppliers and negotiate volume pricing
quiz.explain: High impact and low risk is the leverage quadrant. Competition between many suppliers is your tool to win better price and terms.

modules.title: Planning, Checking and Costing Your Supply
modules.overview: This module gives you the working tools of a purchasing manager. You calculate when to reorder using real lead times, check every delivery before it touches production, score suppliers on facts, and compare suppliers on total cost rather than sticker price before you negotiate.

lessons.title: Lead time, safety stock and the reorder point
objectives: Measure average and worst-case lead time from your own records
Calculate safety stock with the max-minus-average method
Calculate a reorder point and set it up in a spreadsheet
Use a two-bin system for small, cheap materials

blocks.text: Most stockouts are not caused by the supplier alone. They happen because the order was placed too late. The **reorder point** is the stock level that tells you: order now. If you order when stock falls to that level, the new delivery should arrive before you run out, even on a bad week.
Three numbers you need

items: **Usage rate**: how much you use per working day. Use your production records, not a guess.

**Lead time**: the number of working days from the moment you place the order to the moment the material is in your store and checked. Include the time you wait for the supplier to restock, transport, and your own inspection.
**Safety stock**: extra stock you hold to cover days when usage is higher or delivery is slower than normal.

blocks.text: Look back at your last six to ten orders for the material. For each one, count the days from order to usable stock. The average of those is your **average lead time**. The longest one is your **maximum lead time**. Do the same for daily usage: your normal day and your busiest day. A supplier's promise of 'two days' is not your lead time; your records are.

blocks.name: hourglass-with-flowing-sand
blocks.caption: Lead time is the sand running out: your stock must last until the new delivery is ready to use.

blocks.text: The formulas

A simple, widely taught way to set safety stock when you do not have much data is the **max-minus-average** method: safety stock = (maximum daily usage x maximum lead time) minus (average daily usage x average lead time). Then the **reorder point** = (average daily usage x average lead time) + safety stock. More advanced methods use statistics, but this version works well for a small business with a notebook and a few months of records.

blocks.title: Worked example: reorder point for bottles
blocks.context: Amaka, for example, fills an average of 100 bottles a day over six working days. On her busiest days she fills 140. From her last eight bottle orders, delivery took 5 working days on average and 8 days at worst.
steps: Normal demand during lead time: 100 bottles x 5 days = 500 bottles
Worst-case demand during lead time: 140 bottles x 8 days = 1,120 bottles
Safety stock: 1,120 minus 500 = 620 bottles
Reorder point: 500 + 620 = 1,120 bottles
Cash tied up in safety stock at about ₦60 per bottle: 620 x ₦60 = ₦37,200
blocks.result: When Amaka's bottle count falls to 1,120, she orders. On a normal week about 620 bottles will still be on the shelf when the delivery arrives; in the worst week she just avoids running out.

blocks.text: Notice that with this method the reorder point equals maximum usage multiplied by maximum lead time. It is cautious on purpose. If the ₦37,200 tied up in safety stock is too much for your cash, you can choose a smaller buffer, but then write down the risk you are accepting.

Recalculate every few months, and whenever something changes: a new supplier, a big new customer, or a route that has become slower. A reorder point built on last year's usage will be too low once your sales grow, and that is exactly when a stockout hurts most.

blocks.title: One reorder cycle
items: Stock falls to reorder point
Order placed same day
Supplier restocks and dispatches
Delivery checked and stored
Safety stock untouched or partly used
blocks.caption: The reorder point is set so the delivery lands before the shelf is empty.

blocks.text: How much to order each time

The reorder point tells you **when** to order. How much depends on the supplier's minimum order, pack sizes, your storage space, shelf life and cash. A practical rule is to order enough for a fixed period, for example two or four weeks of normal usage, rounded to full packs. Amaka uses 600 bottles a week, so two weeks is 1,200 bottles. Larger orders may earn a discount, which you will weigh in Lesson 3 of this module.
Put it in a sheet

In Google Sheets or Excel, make one row per material with columns: A material, B average daily use, C average lead time, D maximum daily use, E maximum lead time, F safety stock, G reorder point, H current stock, I status. In F2 type =D2*E2-B2*C2. In G2 type =B2*C2+F2. In I2 type =IF(H2<=G2,"ORDER NOW","OK"). Update column H each Friday after counting, and the sheet tells you what to buy.
The two-bin system for small items

For cheap non-critical items such as thread, labels or cable ties, counting is wasted effort. Use **two bins**: keep stock in two containers, and use only from the first. When the first bin is empty, that is your reorder signal; you work from the second bin while the new stock comes. Make each bin hold at least enough for one lead time plus a little extra.

blocks.title: Seasonal and imported materials
blocks.text: For crops harvested once a year, or materials that come by sea, lead time and price change through the year. Ask your supplier which months are hardest, and plan larger orders before those months rather than using one fixed reorder point all year.

takeaways: Lead time runs from placing the order to having checked, usable stock
Safety stock = max usage x max lead time minus average usage x average lead time
Reorder point = average usage x average lead time + safety stock
A weekly count plus a simple sheet tells you exactly what to order
Two bins work well for cheap, non-critical items

activity.title: Calculate two reorder points
steps: Pick your two most critical materials from Module 1
From records, list the lead time of your last six orders and your daily usage on normal and busy days
Calculate safety stock and reorder point for each, showing your working
Build the sheet with the three formulas and enter today's stock count
Mark the reorder level physically on the shelf or container with tape and a label
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your reorder sheet and a photo of the marked shelf

lessons.title: Receiving checks, storage and supplier scorecards
objectives: Run a receiving check on every delivery before it enters stock
Store materials safely using first-expired, first-out
Link supplier batches to your own product batches
Score suppliers with on-time-in-full and a weighted scorecard

blocks.text: A material problem found at the gate costs you a phone call. The same problem found after production costs you the whole batch, and if it reaches a customer, your reputation. The **receiving check** is the moment you compare what arrived with what you ordered and with your spec from Module 1.

blocks.name: package-arrived
blocks.alt: A person receiving a package at the door
blocks.caption: Every delivery is checked before it joins your stock.

blocks.text: A six-step receiving check

items: **Match the paperwork**: compare the delivery note or receipt with your order: material, quantity, price.
**Count or weigh**: count cartons and weigh a few bags on your own scale. A 25 kg bag that weighs 23.5 kg is short by 6%.
**Inspect packaging**: seals intact, no water damage, no torn bags, labels readable, batch or packing date present.
**Check a sample against the spec**: open several containers from different parts of the load, not just the top one, and compare with your reference sample.
**Decide**: accept, accept with a note, or reject. Put doubtful stock in a marked 'HOLD' area, separate from usable stock, until the supplier responds.
**Record**: write the date, supplier, quantity, batch, result and who checked.

blocks.title: From gate to shelf
items: Delivery arrives
Paperwork and count
Sample against spec
Accept, hold or reject
Label and store
Record result
blocks.caption: No material reaches the production area until it has passed every step.

blocks.title: Complain with evidence, quickly
blocks.text: Take photos of short weight on the scale, damaged packs or contamination before you move anything, and send them to the supplier the same day. A complaint a week later, with no photos, is easy to dispute.

Agree the rules for rejected material before the first order, not during the argument. Who collects the rejected goods, and who pays the transport? Will the supplier replace the material, or credit the value against your next order? How many days do you have to report a problem found only when you open the inner bags? Write the answers in your supplier notes or confirm them in a WhatsApp message, so both sides can refer back to them.
Storing materials properly

items: **FIFO and FEFO**: first in, first out, or for materials with expiry dates, first expired, first out. Put new stock behind old stock.
**Off the floor**: keep sacks and cartons on pallets or shelves, away from walls, to reduce damp and pests.
**Cool, dry, shaded**: heat and humidity spoil oils, sugar, flour and many packaging materials.
**Separate**: keep chemicals, cleaning products and fuel well apart from food or cosmetic materials.
**Label**: each container shows the material, supplier, date received and batch.

blocks.text: Traceability: linking batches

**Traceability** means you can say which supplier delivery went into which of your product batches. Give each production batch a code, for example the date plus a letter, and in your production record write the supplier batch or delivery date of each key material used. If a customer complains, you can find the material, check the remaining stock, and talk to the supplier with facts. Larger buyers and regulators increasingly expect this, and it costs only a column in your notebook.
Scoring suppliers on facts

Memory is unfair to suppliers: we remember the last bad delivery and forget ten good ones. The standard measure is **on time in full (OTIF)**: the percentage of deliveries that arrived by the agreed date with the full quantity and passed inspection. If 9 of 12 deliveries met all three conditions, OTIF is 9 divided by 12, which is 75%.

blocks.title: Worked example: a weighted supplier scorecard
blocks.context: Bisi, for example, compares two fabric suppliers over the last school term. She scores each from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) and weights the criteria by what matters most to her uniforms.
steps: Weights: quality 40%, delivery (OTIF) 30%, price 20%, communication 10%
Supplier A scores: quality 4, delivery 3, price 4, communication 5
Supplier B scores: quality 3, delivery 4, price 5, communication 3
blocks.result: Supplier A wins narrowly despite a higher price, because quality carries the most weight for school uniforms. Bisi keeps A as main supplier, tells A that delivery must improve, and keeps a small regular order with B as backup.

blocks.text: Keep a delivery log like the table above, and every quarter turn it into OTIF figures and scorecards. Share the results with each supplier. Good suppliers usually respond well to clear, fair data, and it gives you a calm basis for asking them to improve.

takeaways: Check paperwork, count, packaging and a spread-out sample before accepting
Doubtful stock goes to a separate HOLD area, never into production
Store off the floor, separate chemicals from food materials, use FIFO or FEFO
Record supplier batches against your own batches for traceability
OTIF and a weighted scorecard replace memory with facts

activity.title: Set up your receiving system
steps: Write your six-step receiving checklist on one card and fix it near where deliveries arrive
Mark a HOLD area in your store with tape or a sign
Start a delivery log with the columns shown in the table
Run the check on your next delivery and record the result
Choose four scorecard criteria and weights that suit your product
activity.evidence: A photo of the checklist card and HOLD area, and your first completed delivery log entry

lessons.title: Total cost of ownership and negotiating with suppliers
objectives: Calculate the landed cost per usable unit of a material
Compare suppliers on total cost, not sticker price
Judge whether a quantity discount is worth the cash it ties up
Prepare a supplier negotiation using your BATNA

blocks.text: The cheapest price per kilogram is often not the cheapest material. **Total cost of ownership** (TCO) adds everything it costs you to get a material into production: the price, transport, minimum order effects, waste, extra labour, and the cost of late or failed deliveries. Purchasing professionals compare suppliers on TCO, and so should you.
Landed cost per usable unit

Start with **landed cost**: price plus every cost of getting the material to your door, such as transport, loading, market levies and transfer charges. Then divide by the quantity you can actually use after waste. That gives the **cost per usable unit**, the figure that matters for your product costing.

blocks.title: Worked example: two shea butter suppliers
blocks.context: Funke, for example, compares her Lagos trader with a cheaper processor in the north. She orders 25 kg at a time. Prices are illustrative.
steps: Supplier A (Lagos): ₦2,500 per kg, free delivery. 25 x ₦2,500 = ₦62,500. Waste after straining 1%, so 24.75 kg usable
A's cost per usable kg: ₦62,500 divided by 24.75 = about ₦2,525
Supplier B (north): ₦2,000 per kg, plus ₦7,500 transport. 25 x ₦2,000 + ₦7,500 = ₦57,500
B's waste after straining is 10% (her trial showed grit), so 22.5 kg usable. Extra straining time she values at ₦2,000. Total ₦59,500
B's cost per usable kg: ₦59,500 divided by 22.5 = about ₦2,644
B was also late on 2 of her last 6 orders, which forced emergency buying at a higher price
blocks.result: The supplier that looked 20% cheaper is about ₦119 more expensive per usable kilogram, before counting late deliveries. Funke stays with A, and tells B she would reconsider if the butter came cleaner.

blocks.title: Sticker price versus total cost
items: Sticker price
Total cost of ownership
blocks.caption: Compare suppliers on the right-hand column, because that is what your product actually pays.

blocks.text: Is a quantity discount worth it?

Suppose Supplier A offers ₦2,350 per kg if Funke buys 50 kg instead of 25 kg. Saving: ₦150 x 50 = ₦7,500. But she must pay ₦117,500 at once instead of ₦62,500, so ₦55,000 more cash leaves her business early and sits on the shelf for an extra month. Ask three questions: Do I have the cash without starving other needs? Will the material keep well for that long in my storage conditions? Do I have space? If all three answers are yes, the discount is worth taking. If cash is tight, ₦7,500 is not worth missing a profitable order elsewhere.

blocks.name: handshake-deal
blocks.alt: Two people shaking hands on a deal
blocks.caption: Good negotiation ends with a deal both sides can keep.

blocks.text: Negotiating with suppliers
Price is only one lever. Small producers often gain more from the other ones, and suppliers find them easier to give. Before you talk, decide what you want on each:

items: **Price tiers**: what price at 25 kg, 50 kg, 100 kg?
**Payment terms**: for example half on order and half on delivery, or a few days' credit once trust is built
**Delivery**: fixed delivery day, delivery included, or a faster option for emergencies
**Quality guarantee**: replacement or credit for material that fails the agreed spec
**Priority**: a promise to reserve stock for you during shortages, in return for regular orders

blocks.text: Your strongest preparation is your **BATNA**, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It comes from the Harvard negotiation tradition. In sourcing, your BATNA is usually your approved backup supplier and their price. If you know you can buy at ₦2,550 elsewhere, you can calmly decline a rise to ₦2,700. Without a backup, you have no real alternative, and the supplier can sense it. This is one more reason the backup work in Module 1 pays off.
Running the conversation

items: **Prepare**: write your expected volume for the next three months, your BATNA, the price you hope for and the point at which you will walk away.
**Open with facts and the relationship**: 'I have bought from you every month this year and I expect to double my volume from January.'
**Ask open questions**: 'What would it take to get a better price at 50 kg?' Let the supplier propose first.
**Trade, do not just take**: if they move on price, offer something they value, such as a fixed order day, faster payment or a longer commitment.
**Confirm in writing**: send a short WhatsApp summary of what was agreed the same day, and keep it with your supplier notes.

blocks.title: Protect your money and records
blocks.text: Pay by bank transfer or through a traceable channel such as a business account on Moniepoint, OPay or your bank app, and keep every receipt. Confirm the account name matches the supplier before sending. If a supplier suddenly asks you to pay into a different account, call them on the number you already know before paying.

takeaways: Landed cost includes transport and charges; cost per usable unit also includes waste
A lower sticker price can be the more expensive material
A quantity discount is only worth it if cash, shelf life and space allow
Negotiate payment terms, delivery, quality guarantees and priority, not just price
A tested backup supplier is your BATNA and your negotiating strength

activity.title: Run a total cost comparison
steps: Choose one strategic or leverage material and get current quotes from two suppliers
Calculate landed cost and cost per usable unit for each, using real waste figures from a trial
Note any late or short deliveries from your log
Write down your BATNA and three things you will ask your main supplier for
Hold the conversation and record what was agreed
activity.evidence: Your comparison worksheet and a written note of the agreed terms

quiz.q: A material's average daily use is 20 kg and average lead time is 4 days. The busiest day uses 30 kg and the longest lead time was 6 days. What is the reorder point?
quiz.explain: Safety stock = 30 x 6 minus 20 x 4 = 180 minus 80 = 100 kg. Reorder point = 80 + 100 = 180 kg.

quiz.q: Which time should be counted inside lead time?
options: Only the time the truck is on the road
Only the time the supplier promises
From placing the order until the material is checked and usable in your store
From the day you run out until the next delivery
quiz.explain: Lead time covers the whole wait from order to usable stock, including restocking, transport and your own inspection.

quiz.q: A delivery of sugar arrives with two wet, caked bags out of twenty. What should happen first?
options: Use the wet bags first so they do not waste
Photograph them, place them in the HOLD area and inform the supplier the same day
Accept everything and complain next month
Mix the wet sugar with the dry sugar
quiz.explain: Doubtful stock is separated, documented with photos and reported quickly, so it never enters production and the claim is easy to support.

quiz.q: A supplier made 16 deliveries this year. 12 were on time, in full and passed inspection. What is their OTIF?
quiz.explain: OTIF = deliveries meeting all three conditions divided by total deliveries: 12 divided by 16 = 75%.

quiz.q: Supplier X sells at ₦1,000 per kg with 2% waste. Supplier Y sells at ₦900 per kg plus ₦5,000 transport per 50 kg order, with 12% waste. For a 50 kg order, which is cheaper per usable kg?
options: X, about ₦1,020 per usable kg against about ₦1,136 for Y
Y, because the price per kg is lower
quiz.explain: X: ₦50,000 divided by 49 kg = about ₦1,020. Y: ₦45,000 + ₦5,000 = ₦50,000 divided by 44 kg = about ₦1,136. X is cheaper per usable kilogram.

quiz.q: In a supplier negotiation, what is Funke's BATNA?
options: The lowest price she hopes to get
Her approved backup supplier and the price she can buy at there
quiz.explain: The BATNA is the best alternative if no agreement is reached. In sourcing, that is usually a tested backup supplier and their terms.

modules.title: Growing a Resilient Supply Chain
modules.overview: With the basics in place, you can grow. This module covers buying closer to the source, pooling orders with other producers, the basics of importing, handing purchasing to a trusted person with proper controls, and building the risk register and 90-day plan that make your supply chain resilient.

lessons.title: Buying closer to the source: direct buying, group purchasing and importing
objectives: Decide when buying direct from a producer or importer is worth it
Organise and cost a group purchase fairly between members
Explain the main Incoterms used when importing
Recognise exchange-rate and regulatory risks before importing

blocks.text: Each layer between you and the source adds a margin and a delay. Buying closer to the source, for example from a processor, a factory distributor or directly from abroad, can lower your price and give you better information about quality and availability. It also brings new demands: bigger minimum orders, more cash paid earlier, longer lead times and more of the risk on your side.

blocks.title: Market trader or direct source?
items: Buying from a market trader
Buying direct from the source
blocks.caption: Neither is always better; move closer to the source only when your volume and cash can carry it.

blocks.text: Buying direct makes sense when three things are true: your volume is steady enough to meet the minimum order, you have the cash and storage for larger lots, and the saving remains after you add transport, waste and your own time. If one of the three is missing, a reliable trader is often the better partner.
Group purchasing

If your volume is too small to buy direct, combine it with other producers. A **group purchase** (or buying cooperative) lets several small businesses order together to reach a bulk price, while each stays independent. It works when members use the same material to the same spec and trust the arrangements, which must be written down.

blocks.name: team-up
blocks.alt: People joining hands as a team
blocks.caption: Pooling orders lets small producers buy like a bigger company.

blocks.title: Worked example: five cream makers buy shea butter together
blocks.context: Funke and four other body-cream makers in her WhatsApp producers' group, for example, combine their orders. A processor offers ₦2,150 per kg for 250 kg, against the ₦2,500 they each pay for 25 kg. Transport for the whole load is ₦30,000. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Orders: Funke 80 kg, Chioma 60 kg, Halima 50 kg, Ese 40 kg, Kemi 20 kg. Total 250 kg
Transport shared by weight: ₦30,000 divided by 250 = ₦120 per kg
Landed cost: ₦2,150 + ₦120 = ₦2,270 per kg, a saving of ₦230 per kg against ₦2,500
Funke pays 80 x ₦2,270 = ₦181,600 and saves 80 x ₦230 = ₦18,400 on this order
blocks.result: Every member pays the same landed price per kg, the total collected (₦567,500) exactly covers goods and transport, and each saves about 9%.

items: Write a short agreement: the spec, each member's quantity, how costs are shared, who holds the money and who checks the goods
Collect all money before paying the supplier, into one account, with receipts shared in the group
Weigh each share on delivery in front of members or on video
Agree in advance what happens if the material fails the spec
Rotate or share the coordinator role, and keep records visible to all

blocks.text: Importing: the basics

Some materials, such as certain packaging, machinery parts, fragrance oils or speciality ingredients, may be cheaper or only available abroad. International trade uses the **Incoterms rules** published by the International Chamber of Commerce (the current set is Incoterms 2020) to state who pays for what and where risk passes from seller to buyer. Always agree the Incoterm and the named place in writing.

head: Term
Seller's job
Buyer's job
Watch out for
rows: Make goods available at the seller's premises
Almost everything: loading, export, freight, import, delivery
Cheapest-looking quote, most work and risk for you
Deliver goods loaded on the ship at the named port of shipment
Sea freight, insurance, import clearance, delivery
Sea transport only; risk passes to you once goods are on board
Pay freight and minimum insurance to the named destination port
Import clearance, duties, delivery from the port
Risk still passes to you at loading, even though the seller pays freight
Deliver to your named place with import duties paid
Highest price; check the seller can really clear goods in Nigeria

blocks.name: ship
blocks.caption: Imported materials add weeks of lead time at sea and in clearance.

blocks.text: Importing also exposes you to **exchange-rate risk**. For illustration, if a supplier quotes $2,000 and the rate is ₦1,500 to the dollar, the goods cost ₦3,000,000. If the naira weakens by 10% to ₦1,650 before you pay, the same goods cost ₦3,300,000, an extra ₦300,000 before any freight or duty. Build a margin for this into your costing, and check the current rate on the day you pay.

blocks.title: Check rules before you import
blocks.text: Some imported products must meet Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) conformity requirements, and food, cosmetic and chemical inputs may fall under NAFDAC rules. Ask your bank about the documentation needed for foreign payments, and speak with a licensed customs agent before your first order. Never pay a foreign supplier you have not verified, and start with a sample shipment.

takeaways: Buy direct only when volume, cash and storage can carry the larger lots
A written group purchase lets small producers reach bulk prices fairly
Share group transport by weight so everyone pays the same landed cost per kg
Incoterms state who pays and when risk passes; under CIF, risk passes at loading
Imports add exchange-rate, lead-time and regulatory risk

activity.title: Test a group purchase
steps: Identify a material you share with at least two other producers
Ask one larger supplier for prices at your single volume and at the combined volume
Calculate the landed cost per kg and each member's payment, sharing transport by weight
Draft a one-page group buying agreement with spec, quantities, money handling and checking
activity.evidence: Your cost split sheet and the draft agreement

lessons.title: Delegating purchasing with clear roles and controls
objectives: Separate the duties of requesting, approving, receiving and paying
Set approval limits and an approved supplier list
Recognise and prevent conflicts of interest in buying
Train a helper to buy and receive to your standard

blocks.text: As you grow, you cannot go to the market for every purchase. Handing buying to a staff member, family member or agent frees your time, but it also hands them your money and your quality. The answer is not to avoid delegating. It is to delegate with a clear process and simple controls, the way established companies do.

blocks.name: team-assignment
blocks.alt: A manager assigning tasks to team members
blocks.caption: Clear roles let others buy for you without risking quality or cash.

blocks.text: The purchasing cycle and separation of duties

blocks.title: The purchasing cycle
items: Request
Approve
Order
Receive and check
Pay
Review supplier
blocks.caption: Wherever possible, different people handle ordering, receiving and paying, so no one can both buy and confirm their own purchase.

blocks.text: **Separation of duties** is a basic internal control: the person who places an order should not be the only person who confirms it arrived, and ideally not the one who pays. In a two-person business, it can be as simple as: your buyer orders, you or another person counts the delivery against the order, and payment goes out from the business account only after the count matches.
Approval limits and an approved supplier list

blocks.title: Worked example: Bisi's buying rules for her assistant
blocks.context: Bisi, for example, hires Tunde to handle buying for her uniform workshop. She writes these rules on one page and both sign it.
steps: Approved supplier list: two fabric suppliers, one trimmings supplier and one packaging supplier, with phone numbers and agreed prices
Up to ₦50,000 per order from an approved supplier at the agreed price: Tunde can order without asking
₦50,001 to ₦300,000: Tunde sends the quote on WhatsApp and waits for Bisi's written 'approved'
Above ₦300,000, any new supplier or any price above the agreed price: Bisi decides, after at least two quotes
Receiving: Bisi's senior tailor counts and checks every delivery against the order using the receiving checklist
Payment: by transfer from the business account only, after the receiving record is signed
blocks.result: Tunde can handle routine buying quickly, while large, unusual or new purchases still come to Bisi, and no single person can order, receive and pay alone.

blocks.text: A **purchase order** (PO) does not need special software. A numbered WhatsApp message or a page in a duplicate book that states the supplier, material, spec, quantity, price, delivery date and order number is enough. The receiver checks against it, and the payer pays against it.

head: Step
Two-person business
Three or more people
rows: Owner or bookkeeper, from the business account

blocks.title: Cash for market trips
blocks.text: If your buyer must pay cash in the market, give a fixed float, for example enough for one week of small purchases. They return receipts and the remaining cash at the end of the week, and you top the float back up to the same amount. Any gap between receipts plus cash and the float is discussed at once, not left to grow.
Conflicts of interest

A **conflict of interest** exists when a buyer's personal interest could influence a business decision: a supplier who is a relative, a 'thank you' cash gift for each order, or a buyer who quietly owns part of a supplier. It does not always mean wrongdoing, but it must be declared. A common warning sign is a buyer who resists getting other quotes, or a price that slowly rises above the market while quality stays the same.

items: Ask everyone who buys for you to declare any personal link to a supplier, in writing
State plainly that gifts or commissions from suppliers must be reported or refused
Get fresh quotes for strategic and leverage items at least once or twice a year
Compare your buyer's prices with what you hear in the market from time to time

blocks.text: Training your buyer

items: Explain the why: show the BOM and how a 10% price rise or a bad batch affects profit
Walk through each spec with the reference samples in hand
Do the first two market trips together, then let them lead while you watch
Practise the receiving check on a real delivery, including a pretend rejection
Agree what to do in an emergency: who to call and what they may decide alone
Review the delivery log and scorecards together each month

blocks.text: Keep the monthly review short and practical: look at the delivery log, the OTIF figure for each supplier, any rejections, and any price changes since last month. Ask your buyer what they are hearing in the market about shortages or new suppliers. People closest to the market often see problems first, and a buyer who feels trusted to raise them is one of your best early warning systems.

blocks.title: Keep supplier knowledge in the business
blocks.text: Keep supplier contacts, specs, prices and the delivery log in a shared sheet or notebook that belongs to the business, not in one person's phone. If your buyer leaves, the knowledge stays.

takeaways: Delegate buying with a written process instead of avoiding it
Separate ordering, receiving and paying wherever you can
Approval limits plus an approved supplier list speed up routine buying safely
Personal links and gifts from suppliers must be declared
Train with real samples and real deliveries, then review together monthly

activity.title: Write your purchasing rules
steps: Draw your purchasing cycle and write who does each step today
Set approval limits in naira that suit your business size
List your approved suppliers with agreed prices
Write a one-paragraph conflict of interest declaration and gifts rule
Plan two training sessions for the person who buys or receives for you
activity.evidence: Your signed one-page purchasing rules and approved supplier list

lessons.title: Your supply risk register and 90-day resilience plan
objectives: Score supply risks by likelihood and impact
Choose a mitigation for each high risk
Build a 90-day plan to reduce your biggest vulnerability
Present your sourcing practice confidently to larger buyers

blocks.text: **Resilience** is your supply chain's ability to keep production going when something goes wrong, and to recover quickly when it cannot. You cannot prevent fuel price jumps, road closures or a factory breakdown. You can know in advance which of these would hurt most and prepare a response. The tool for this is a **risk register**.

blocks.name: master-plan
blocks.alt: A person standing in front of a large plan on a board
blocks.caption: A risk register turns worry into a written list of actions.

blocks.text: Scoring risks

List what could go wrong with each critical material: supplier stops trading, price jumps, quality drops, transport is disrupted, the material becomes seasonal or scarce. Give each risk two scores from 1 (low) to 5 (high): **likelihood**, how probable it is in the next year, and **impact**, how badly it would hurt production, quality or profit. Multiply them. A score of 15 or more needs action now; 8 to 14 needs a plan; below 8 you watch.

blocks.title: Worked example: Amaka's risk register
blocks.context: Amaka, for example, scores the main risks to her zobo business using her map from Module 1 and her delivery log.
steps: Only bottle distributor fails to deliver for two weeks: likelihood 4 x impact 5 = 20
Hibiscus price spikes before the next harvest: likelihood 3 x impact 4 = 12
Sugar price rises sharply: likelihood 4 x impact 3 = 12
Label printer loses her design file: likelihood 2 x impact 3 = 6
Mitigation for bottles (20): qualify a second bottle source, and hold the 620-bottle safety stock from Module 2, costing about ₦37,200 of cash
Mitigation for hibiscus (12): buy a larger stock earlier when prices are lower, if storage keeps it dry
blocks.result: The bottle risk scores highest by far, so it becomes the focus of her 90-day plan. The printer risk is fixed today in five minutes by saving her own copy of the file.

head: Response
What it means
Example
rows: Approve a second supplier and give it regular orders
Second bottle distributor at 20 to 30% of volume
Hold extra safety stock of the material
Two weeks of bottles on the shelf
Approve an alternative material in advance
A second bottle shape with matching cap and label size
Monthly forecast and reserved stock agreement

blocks.text: Every response has a cost, so match the effort to the score. Amaka's 620 bottles of safety stock tie up about ₦37,200. A two-week bottle shortage would stop sales of about 1,200 bottles, which at her selling price is many times that amount in lost income, plus angry shop customers. For the bottle risk, the buffer is clearly worth it. For ginger, a cheap and widely sold material, the same spending would be wasted.
An emergency card for each critical material
For each material scoring 15 or more, write a small emergency card and keep it where you and your staff can find it. If the supplier fails, nobody has to think from scratch under pressure.

items: Backup supplier names and phone numbers, and what they last charged
How many days current stock will last at normal use
Any approved substitute material and what must change, such as labels or caps
Which customers to inform first, and what to tell them
Who in the business may make emergency purchases, and up to what amount

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: 90 days to reduce one risk
items: Days 1 to 15: find options
Days 16 to 30: samples and trials
Days 31 to 60: first real orders
Days 61 to 80: split regular orders
Days 81 to 90: review and update
blocks.caption: One clearly chosen risk, worked on week by week, beats a long list nobody acts on.

items: **Days 1 to 15**: list at least three possible alternative suppliers from markets, trade associations, producer groups and online directories. Call each and send your spec.
**Days 16 to 30**: request samples or buy small trials. Test against your spec and reference sample, and record results.
**Days 31 to 60**: place one or two real orders with the best new option. Measure lead time and run your receiving check.
**Days 61 to 80**: if it passes, split regular orders, for example 70% main and 30% backup, and build your safety stock to the planned level.
**Days 81 to 90**: review the risk score again, update your map, reorder sheet and scorecards, and choose the next risk.

blocks.text: Showing buyers you are reliable

Supermarkets, hotels, schools and distributors worry about suppliers who cannot deliver consistently. Your sourcing work is evidence. Prepare a short sourcing statement for proposals, for example: 'We hold approved primary and backup suppliers for our key materials, check every delivery against written specifications, keep batch records, and hold safety stock for critical materials.' Only write what is true, and be ready to show the records.

blocks.title: Review on a rhythm
blocks.text: Supply risks change. Review your register every three months and after any serious disruption. Add what happened, how you handled it and what you would do differently. Over a year, this record becomes one of the most valuable documents in your business.

takeaways: Score each risk by likelihood x impact, and act first on the highest
Responses: add a source, buffer, substitute, strengthen, or accept and watch
A 90-day plan works on one major risk at a time, week by week
Your sourcing records are evidence of reliability for larger buyers

activity.title: Build your risk register
steps: List at least six supply risks for your critical materials
Score likelihood and impact from 1 to 5 and multiply
Choose a response for every risk scoring 8 or more
Write a 90-day plan with dates for your highest-scoring risk
Write a three-sentence sourcing statement you could put in a proposal
activity.evidence: Your scored risk register, dated 90-day plan and sourcing statement

quiz.q: Four producers share a 200 kg order at ₦1,800 per kg with ₦16,000 transport. Ngozi takes 50 kg. What should she pay?
quiz.explain: Transport per kg = ₦16,000 divided by 200 = ₦80. Landed cost = ₦1,880 per kg. 50 x ₦1,880 = ₦94,000.

quiz.q: Under CIF, the seller pays sea freight to Lagos. When does the risk of loss pass to the buyer?
options: When the goods reach Lagos port
When the goods are loaded on board at the port of shipment
When the goods reach the buyer's store
quiz.explain: Under CIF the seller pays freight and minimum insurance, but risk passes to the buyer once the goods are on board at the port of shipment.

quiz.q: Bisi's assistant orders fabric, receives it and pays for it alone. What is the main weakness?
options: No separation of duties, so errors or dishonesty can go unnoticed
quiz.explain: When one person orders, confirms and pays, nobody independently checks that what was paid for actually arrived at the right price and quality.

quiz.q: A supplier risk has likelihood 3 and impact 5. Using the course's scoring guide, what should happen?
options: Ignore it, the likelihood is only 3
Act now, the score of 15 is in the action band
Watch only, because it is below 20
quiz.explain: 3 x 5 = 15, which reaches the 'act now' threshold of 15 or more.

quiz.q: Your buyer's prices for thread have risen steadily for six months while market prices stayed flat, and the buyer refuses to get other quotes. What is the best first step?
options: Ignore it because thread is a small item
Get independent quotes yourself and ask the buyer to declare any links to the supplier
quiz.explain: These are warning signs of a possible conflict of interest. Gather facts with independent quotes and ask for a declaration before deciding anything.

quiz.q: Which first step best fits Days 1 to 15 of a 90-day plan to reduce dependence on one bottle supplier?
options: Move all orders to a new supplier at once
List and contact at least three alternative suppliers and send them your spec
quiz.explain: The plan starts by finding options. Trials, real orders and split ordering follow only after candidates are identified and tested.

finalQuiz.q: Which material in a bill of materials deserves most attention on price?
options: The one with the largest share of material cost
The one with the cheapest unit price
The one bought from the nearest market
finalQuiz.explain: A price change on a material with a large cost share moves your total cost the most.

finalQuiz.q: A material is essential, has only one supplier and cannot be swapped within a week. It is:
options: A critical material and a single point of failure
finalQuiz.explain: Essential, hard to replace and single-sourced: losing that one supplier would stop production.

finalQuiz.q: Which quadrant of the Kraljic matrix is best handled by comparing quotes and negotiating volume prices?
finalQuiz.explain: Leverage items have high spend and many suppliers, so competition gives you bargaining power.

finalQuiz.q: Why should a small producer's spec use checks like looking, smelling, weighing and trial batches?
options: Because she must be able to verify the spec herself on every delivery
finalQuiz.explain: A spec is only useful if the person receiving goods can actually check it.

finalQuiz.q: Average use is 50 units a day, average lead time 4 days, maximum use 70 units and maximum lead time 6 days. What is the safety stock?
finalQuiz.explain: 70 x 6 = 420; 50 x 4 = 200; safety stock = 420 minus 200 = 220 units. The reorder point would be 200 + 220 = 420.

finalQuiz.q: Which item is best managed with a two-bin system?
options: Imported fragrance oil from one supplier
A seasonal crop bought once a year
finalQuiz.explain: Two bins suit cheap, easy-to-buy, non-critical items where counting is not worth the effort.

finalQuiz.q: During a receiving check you find some bags are under weight. Which action is correct?
options: Accept quietly to keep the relationship
Weigh and photograph the bags, record it and inform the supplier the same day
Return the whole delivery without speaking to the supplier
Use the short bags first and say nothing
finalQuiz.explain: Evidence recorded at once, and reported the same day, makes the claim fair and easy to resolve.

finalQuiz.q: Supplier A scores quality 5, delivery 3 and Supplier B scores quality 3, delivery 5. Weights are quality 60% and delivery 40%. Who scores higher?
A supplier offers 10% off if you double your order size. What must you check first?
options: Only whether the discount is above 5%
Cash available, shelf life in your storage, and space
finalQuiz.explain: A discount only helps if the extra cash, storage time and space do not cost you more than you save.

finalQuiz.q: What gives you the most strength when a key supplier announces a price rise?
options: An approved backup supplier with a known price
finalQuiz.explain: A tested backup is your BATNA: a real alternative that lets you decline poor terms calmly.

finalQuiz.q: A WhatsApp group of producers wants to buy together. Which rule protects everyone most?
options: Members pay after the goods are shared
A written agreement on spec, quantities, cost sharing and checking, with money collected first and receipts shared
Transport is paid by whoever lives nearest
finalQuiz.explain: Written terms, money collected before ordering and visible receipts prevent most disputes in group buying.

finalQuiz.q: Which risk should come first in a 90-day plan?
finalQuiz.explain: Scores are 4, 9, 20 and 5. The risk scoring 20 is the highest and needs action first.

capstone.title: Supply Chain Resilience Plan
capstone.brief: A short written plan, in a notebook or Google Sheet, that shows your key materials with primary and backup suppliers, reorder points for your two most critical materials based on real lead times, and a dated 90-day plan to reduce your single biggest sourcing vulnerability.
steps: Write the bill of materials for your main product and draw your supply map, circling single points of failure
Rank all materials with ABC analysis and place them on the Kraljic matrix
For each key material, list the primary supplier and at least one backup option, with contact details and spec
Calculate safety stock and reorder point for your top two critical materials, using at least six past lead times
Score your supply risks by likelihood and impact and pick the highest
Write a dated 90-day plan to reduce that risk and start the first step
evidence: Bill of materials with cost shares and a photo of the supply map
Key materials list with primary and backup suppliers
Reorder point calculations for two critical materials, with working shown
Written spec for at least one strategic material
Dated 90-day plan with the first step completed
